text.p: Italian textile group Marzotto's shock move to call off a mega-merger with industrial holding HPI was described by the Italian press on Sunday as an earthquake in the country's financial world. Marzotto cited "irreconcilable organisational and financial differences" in a joint statement with HPI on Saturday for deciding not to go ahead with a fusion that would have created one of the biggest textiles and clothing companies in the world.

"Marzotto says no to Cuccia", La Repubblica said, echoing other papers who said the move was a second major failure for 90-year-old Enrico Cuccia, grand old man of Italian finance and honorary chairman of deal-making Milan merchant bank Mediobanca.
The deal would have created an 8.24 trillion lire ($4.8 billion) group uniting a host of top names like German menswear label Hugo Boss, Giorgio Armani and sportswear maker Fila.

Car maker Fiat and Mediobanca were to have held big stakes and Fiat chairman Cesare Romiti's son Maurizio was to have been managing director of the new group, dubbed "big GIM", for Gruppo Industriale Marzotto.
"The Marzotto board noted with regret that obstacles which had arisen were such as to call off the merger. The HPI board had also noted the decision with regret," the statement said.

It said the board of Marzotto halted the deal with Holding Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI), an industrial holding recently spun off from financial holding Gemina, due to irreconcilable differences after a preparatory review.

These were over "the principles of organisation, sharing of responsibility, and procedures for directing and controlling group companies" and "the group's financial policy goals, and in particular its proposed use of risk capital and lending facilities," the statement said. It gave no further details.
There was press speculation that Pietro Marzotto, head of the family-run textiles firm, was worried about losing control of a company which has been in business for over 160 years.
"The abrupt failure of the merger may seem strange to foreign observers but this is Italy so there's nothing too abnormal about it," said one industry source who declined to be named.

"There are circumstances involved here which are outside the control of the two groups," he said without elaborating. "But Marzotto will continue its aim for international growth and possible future alliances can never be ruled out."

Marzotto, which had been due to hold a shareholders' meeting on May 21 ahead of share swaps in July that would have given birth to GIM, said the board concluded that the merger proposal scheduled to be put to the meeting should be withdrawn.
Analysts were initially upbeat, saying the deal looked good when the ambitious merger plan was announced early in March.
Besides clothing, GIM would have owned Italy's second largest publisher, Rizzoli Corriere della Sera (RCS).
Fiat was expected to have been the biggest shareholder with a 17.3 percent stake, followed by the Marzotto family with 12.4 percent and Mediobanca with 10.5 percent.

Analysts said the hand of Cuccia was clearly behind the deal which was to have succeeded where the collapse of a former mega-merger failed. Instead, the new unexpected turn of events appeared to show Cuccia had lost his Midas touch.
The HPI-Marzotto plan followed the collapse of the so-called "SuperGemina" deal hatched by Cuccia in 1995 to bundle Gemina's interests with the former Ferruzzi agri-chemicals empire.
After the deal was abandoned, following the discovery of huge losses at RCS, Ferruzzi was renamed Compart and Gemina's core industrial interests hived off into HPI.
Marzotto shares closed on Friday in Milan 2.28 percent lower at 12,408 lire while HPI stock ended 0.56 percent lower at 928.1 lire on a firmer stock market. ($=1,711 lire)
